description: Разработка автономный фоновый демон мониторинга телеметрии экипажа и среды отсека.
summary: Near Mars, a message to Earth takes 3 to 22 minutes one way, so a crew must decide alone whether someone is fit for a spacewalk. Fatigue makes that decision unreliable: tired people keep feeling "fine" while their performance falls. MIRROR is a 90-second check that runs in any browser, offline. The crew member first predicts their own reaction time, then takes four quick checks: a reaction test based on the Psychomotor Vigilance Test used on the ISS, a traced spiral for hand steadiness, and a fading-ring test of contrast vision. MIRROR shows the perception gap — how much slower they are than they believe — and gives a GO, RE-CHECK or NO-GO for a spacewalk, docking and routine work. Today's Earth–Mars signal time is computed live from NASA JPL orbital elements.
details:
What it does

MIRROR measures the perception gap: the difference between how fast a crew member believes they are and how fast they really are. A large gap means the person cannot feel their own fatigue — the most dangerous state before a risky task.

How it works

1. Predict: the crew member sets their expected reaction time in milliseconds and rates fatigue on the seven-point Samn-Perelli scale.

2. Measure: four taps on a counter that appears after a random pause (the principle of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test), then a traced Archimedean spiral scored as the average distance from the lane centre.

3. See: a Landolt ring on grey that fades in eight steps; the score is the faintest ring read correctly.

4. Decide: the perception gap = (measured − predicted) ÷ predicted, and a GO, RE-CHECK or NO-GO for a spacewalk, docking and routine work.

The mission view shows today's Earth–Mars light time, real sourced facts about medical emergencies far from Earth, and what the crew does on a NO-GO (hand the task over, nap and re-check, check CO2, report vision changes). Sending a report to Earth is a simulation of the real signal delay; nothing leaves the device. On a real mission a short summary would go by radio through NASA's Deep Space Network.

Benefits

No extra hardware, no internet, about 90 seconds. Prediction and measurement use the same unit, so the gap is a fair comparison. The same check fits pilots, surgeons, drivers and shift workers on Earth.

Tools and languages

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no frameworks or libraries; a 50-line Node.js server lets an iPad open the app over local Wi-Fi. English and Russian interface. Tested on a laptop, an interactive whiteboard and an iPad.

Limits

The four-tap test is a short demonstration, not the validated 3- or 5-minute PVT. GO and NO-GO limits are prototype values for flight surgeons to confirm. Touchscreens add delay, so each screen gets its own rested reference.
